newsitem.title: USA: Lighter moments intrude in Miami smoke trial.
newsitem.headline: Lighter moments intrude in Miami smoke trial.

text.p: The landmark trial is a deadly serious affair about the health effects of cigarette smoke, but lighter moments have intruded into the $5 billion anti-tobacco lawsuit now being tried in Miami.

Talking torsos, fried chicken and "Gummi Bears" candy have all figured in preparations for the trial of Broin vs. Philip Morris et al, in which 60,000 non-smoking airline flight attendants are suing nine cigarette companies for maladies they claim were caused by smoke from passengers' cigarettes.

As jury selection got under way this week, one potential panellist likened the flight attendants suing cigarette companies over secondhand smoke to a hearty eater suing a fast-food chain over fried chicken.

"You're saying that if I had high cholesterol, I should sue Kentucky Fried Chicken," the woman, who was later dismissed, said to plaintiffs' attorney Stanley Rosenblatt as they discussed the case's merits.

In a pretrial hearing last week, Rosenblatt interrupted a tobacco attorney's discussion of what could be included in opening arguments with the Delphic remark: "I won't mention Gummi Bears in my opening statement."
The interjection was a biting reference to part of a taped deposition taken by Rosenblatt's firm that made its way onto the national television show "60 Minutes."

The tape, which led to the tobacco companies' request for a gag order, showed Philip Morris Cos. Inc. President James Morgan saying tobacco is no more addictive than Gummi Bears, a popular candy of which he is fond.
A big question has been whether presiding Judge Robert Kaye is himself a smoker. Courthouse workers said they had never seen Kaye smoking, but the judge refused to comment.
"I'm not going to answer that. I'm not going to say anything prejudicial," he said when asked.
One attorney said he believed the judge had once smoked, but had quit many years ago. "I'm sure he quit cold turkey. He's a tough guy," the attorney said.
But Kaye is not unsympathetic to users of tobacco products. During a pretrial hearing, he leaned down from the bench and said to a table of tobacco attorneys, "Do you need a smoke break?"
The attorneys politely declined.
Kaye, who spent years working as a radio reporter, has stopped short of gagging attorneys but has set limits on the news media.
He has allowed one courtroom television camera, which provides a closed-circuit feed to the media room in the 1920s-era courthouse in downtown Miami.
Kaye ordered that jurors' faces not be taped or photographed at any time.

As a result, those in the press room watched as headless torsos of potential jurors -- most notably that of a young female in a low-cut black blouse -- responded to attorneys' questions about cigarettes, employment and secondhand smoke.
The court has also set a dress code for journalists in a trial expected to last for most of the hot Miami summer, banning among other things see-through shirts, baseball caps and shorts.
The trial is expected to be heard by a jury of six, plus as many as 12 alternates, who will not sit in the typical jury room.
The Dade County courthouse's jury area normally is plastered with the typical range of anti-smoking signs found in public buildings, such as "This is a NO SMOKING area."
But Kaye toured the area on Friday -- saying "I learned very early in my career 'Always check the jury room'" -- and ordered that all of the red signs be taken down.
He envisioned the pool of jurors sitting in the jury room for hours on end surrounded by the placards.
"I don't want them to sit there and stare across the room (at the signs) ... It could be prejudicial," the judge said.
